task.goal: Communicate a community center's energy-saving options without fear tactics, misleading savings numbers or assuming everyone controls the building.
hard_constraints: One printed poster and take-home card; no app or personalized usage data.
Separate actions available to visitors from those only staff can take.
Check whether readers identify one feasible action and understand uncertainty in any savings estimate.
task.available_resources: Existing building policies and verified aggregate energy figures.
task.expected_result: An honest communication mechanism and critique.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A clear menu of actions by role
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use one printed poster and a take-home card with two clearly separated sections: “Visitors can” and “Staff only.” The mechanism is to make authority and feasibility visible before asking anyone to act. Each listed action must be permitted by existing building policy. Visitor options might include switching off designated user-controlled equipment after use or reporting an equipment problem; include these only where policy supports them. Staff options could cover approved scheduling, maintenance or operating adjustments. Visitors are never asked to change shared heating, cooling or safety equipment.

The poster invites readers to choose one action that fits their visit. The card repeats the role labels and action menu, so it remains usable away from the poster. Include a respectful statement that some people have no suitable action during a particular visit.

Use verified aggregate energy figures only as building context, with their period and unit. Explicitly distinguish measured consumption from predicted savings: “This is the building’s recorded use; it does not tell us what your action would save.” Omit action-level savings numbers unless the supplied materials support them and their uncertainty.

Implementation needs a policy review, a short selection of permitted actions, plain-language editing and printing. It assumes the policies identify at least one practical visitor action and one staff action. Its strength is immediate clarity; its limit is that recognizing an action may not lead to doing it. A menu can also imply that every action has equal impact, so avoid rankings unsupported by evidence.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare a draft poster-and-card pair with a simple pair containing the same actions in an ungrouped list. Ask six to eight visitors and two staff members to identify one action they could take, explain who controls it, and describe what the energy figure does and does not establish. Alternate which version readers see first. Revise or reject the role-menu mechanism if readers still select unauthorized actions or interpret building consumption as promised personal savings. This small check assesses comprehension and feasibility, not actual energy reduction.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A practical boundary-and-handoff guide
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Build one printed poster and a take-home card around three questions: “Is this under your control?”, “Does building policy allow the change?”, and “If not, who can help?” The mechanism is a decision guide that converts uncertainty about control into either a permitted visitor action or an appropriate staff handoff.

The visitor path ends with a short set of policy-supported actions. A separate, explicitly labeled “Staff only” path identifies matters requiring staff judgment, such as changes to shared equipment or operating schedules. If an existing reporting route is documented, print it on both pieces. A report is framed as a request for assessment, not an instruction that staff must implement. Where no reporting route exists, use an existing staffed contact point only if the policies establish one; otherwise omit the handoff and explain that the item requires staff action.

The take-home card reproduces the complete guide rather than relying on a link or app. Use welcoming language such as “Choose what fits your visit.” Do not imply responsibility for equipment or conditions readers cannot control.

A small evidence note distinguishes verified building-wide consumption from uncertain savings. If presenting an estimate supported by the materials, state its conditions and that actual savings may differ; otherwise state that savings have not been quantified.

Implementation requires mapping existing policies into a few decisions and checking that any named contact route is current. This approach assumes visitors sometimes encounter ambiguous situations. Its advantage is handling those situations directly. Its limits are reading effort and dependence on staff availability; additional reports could also create work without producing energy savings.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the guide with a simple role-separated action list using the same underlying information. Give six to eight readers two short scenarios drawn from actual policies: one involving permitted visitor control and one requiring staff involvement. Ask what they would do, then ask each to name one feasible action from their own visit and explain the savings uncertainty. The mechanism is challenged if the guide causes more wrong turns, unauthorized changes or confusion than the list. Inspect staff workload implications before printing.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Evidence labels that distinguish facts from possibilities
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Organize one printed poster and its take-home card around three evidence labels: “Measured here,” “Possible actions,” and “What remains uncertain.” The primary mechanism is explicit separation of observation from prediction, allowing readers to consider energy-saving options without treating every suggestion as a quantified promise.

“Measured here” presents a verified aggregate figure with its unit, measurement period and building scope. Choose a figure that can be explained briefly; do not manufacture comparisons or household equivalents. “Possible actions” has visibly separate “Visitors” and “Staff only” subsections, each containing only policy-supported options. The invitation is to choose one feasible action, with no requirement to pledge or claim savings. “What remains uncertain” explains that a building total cannot establish the savings from one person’s action, and that occupancy, weather or operating conditions may affect consumption.

If supplied materials contain a defensible savings estimate, place its assumptions and uncertainty beside the number, with comparable visual prominence. Do not create a range merely to appear cautious. If no estimate is supported, print “We cannot quantify the savings from this action using the available figures.” The card preserves the labels, role separation and uncertainty statement so the message survives being taken home.

Implementation needs verification of the selected figure, policy screening of actions, layout work and printing. It assumes readers can understand a short numeric explanation when units and scope are clear. Its strength is transparent evidence; its limits are that the energy figure may distract from action, and explicit uncertainty could be mistaken for evidence that actions are ineffective. Wording should distinguish unknown magnitude from demonstrated ineffectiveness.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare this pair with a plain poster-and-card pair containing identical facts, actions and caveats in ordinary paragraphs. Ask six to eight readers to identify one feasible action and its authorized role, then explain whether the measured figure predicts their action’s savings. Include a question about whether “unquantified” means “no benefit.” Reject or revise the evidence-label mechanism if it adds confusion, obscures action choices or fails to reduce false savings claims relative to the plain version. This checks communication, not realized savings.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Turn an allowed action into a cue-linked plan
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use one printed poster and a take-home card to help readers connect an authorized action to a specific moment: “When ___ happens, I can ___, if building policy permits.” The mechanism is prospective planning: remembering an action at the relevant moment may be easier than remembering a general energy-saving message. This differs from simply identifying an option, although its effectiveness here remains untested.

The poster provides two clearly separated planning areas, “Visitors” and “Staff only,” with a few actions verified against existing policies. Each example pairs an action with an observable cue. For instance, only if policy permits, a visitor example could connect finishing use of designated equipment with switching it off. Staff examples use policy-supported operating or maintenance tasks. Neither area invites visitors to adjust shared building systems.

The card repeats the role boundaries, examples and evidence note, with an optional blank sentence readers can complete privately. It requires no submission, pledge, app or usage record. Include “If nothing fits your visit, you do not need to make a plan.” Avoid guilt or promises that an individual action will noticeably change the building total.

Print “Savings from this plan have not been quantified” unless the supplied materials support an estimate. Any supported estimate must carry its conditions and uncertainty beside it; verified aggregate consumption alone cannot establish action-level savings.

Implementation requires a policy review, selection of reliable cues, plain-language layout and printing. It assumes at least one permitted action has a recognizable occasion for use. Its main limitation is that a well-formed plan can still be forgotten or impractical; it also cannot establish which actions save most energy.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the planning pair with a simple role-separated list containing the same actions and evidence note. With six to eight readers, ask each to identify one feasible action, its authorized role and when they could perform it. After a brief unrelated activity, ask them to recall the occasion and explain whether any savings amount is established. Revise or reject the planning mechanism if it produces unauthorized plans, unrealistic cues or more false certainty than the list, or offers no apparent recall advantage. This small check can expose communication failures; it cannot demonstrate energy savings.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Practice a choice, then check the explanation
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use one printed poster and a take-home card as a brief rehearsal: readers consider an everyday situation, choose a response, then check an explanation. The mechanism is active retrieval with corrective feedback. Practicing a choice may help readers recognize an appropriate action during a later visit; whether it improves understanding here is unknown.

Build two short situations from existing building policies. Clearly label one “Visitors” and the other “Staff only.” Each offers a permitted response and a plausible mistake. For example, if policy supports it, contrast switching off designated user-controlled equipment after use with changing shared controls. Explain the consequence of each choice neutrally, without shaming readers. Put explanations below the poster questions and on the reverse of the card. Both pieces include the complete exercise and remain independently usable.

Add a savings question: “Would choosing this action tell us how much energy this building saved?” Explain that verified aggregate consumption alone cannot establish the contribution of that action. If the available materials support an estimate, reproduce its conditions and uncertainty beside it; otherwise state that the savings amount is unknown. Do not invent numerical distractors that could be remembered as claims.

Finish with an optional transfer prompt: “Which permitted action could fit your visit?” Explicitly allow “None today.” Staff retain responsibility for shared systems.

Implementation requires policy review, two realistic situations, short answer explanations, layout and printing. It assumes readers will engage with a brief exercise. Its limits are participation effort, possible embarrassment from a quiz-like tone, and readers remembering a mistaken option. Use an invitation to practice, with corrections immediately accessible.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the exercise pair with a simple role-separated action list containing the same information. Ask six to eight readers to inspect one version, alternating assignment. Then present a different policy-grounded situation and ask each reader to identify one personally feasible action, distinguish visitor from staff authority, and explain what savings can be inferred. Revise or reject the exercise if readers repeat its mistaken options, cannot transfer the lesson, or show no clearer understanding than readers of the list. This checks comprehension, not energy reduction.

EXPAND.title: Attach an action to a familiar moment
EXPAND.proposal:
Use one printed poster and a take-home card to help readers form a simple cue-and-action plan: “When ___ happens during my visit, I can ___.” The mechanism is connecting a permitted action to a recognizable moment, reducing the need to remember a general energy-saving message later.

The poster provides two or three policy-verified examples under “Visitors,” with a separate “Staff only” section containing staff routines. For example, an end-of-session cue could lead to switching off designated equipment, but only if the policies explicitly permit visitors to do so. Staff examples must likewise reflect authorized responsibilities. Each example includes a boundary: which equipment, conditions or decisions require staff involvement.

The card repeats the role-separated examples and includes an optional blank cue-and-action sentence. Readers keep it; nobody collects plans or personal usage information. Invite readers to choose a plan only if an appropriate opportunity exists. Avoid pledges, competition and claims that every visit offers an energy-saving opportunity.

Print a short evidence statement on both pieces: verified building consumption describes aggregate use, while the savings from an individual plan remain unquantified unless the supplied materials support an estimate. Any supported estimate must carry its assumptions and uncertainty beside it.

Implementation requires a policy review, identification of recurring moments and printing. It assumes at least one permitted action has a recognizable cue. Its advantage is making an action easier to remember when relevant. Its limits are that routines vary and a memorable cue can encourage an inappropriate action unless the boundary is equally clear. This approach does not establish that remembered actions produce measurable building savings.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare the draft pair with a simple role-separated list containing the same actions and evidence statement. Ask six readers to name one feasible action, its trigger and who may perform it. After a brief unrelated conversation, ask what they would do in a relevant situation and in a similar situation where permission does not apply. Ask whether the building figure predicts their savings. Revise or reject the cue mechanism if recall does not improve, readers overgeneralize permission, or savings uncertainty becomes less clear. This is a comprehension and recall check, not proof of changed behavior.

EXPAND.title: Teach boundaries through contrasting situations
EXPAND.proposal:
Make one printed poster and a take-home card a compact set of worked situations. The mechanism is learning by comparison: readers see how a small change in circumstances changes which action is feasible and who has authority.

Use two paired situations derived from existing building policies. One pair might contrast equipment explicitly designated for visitor control with equipment reserved for staff, if those categories exist locally. Explain the decisive difference in one sentence. Label visitor actions and staff-only actions explicitly in separate sections; do not rely on readers to infer the distinction from the stories. The card reproduces the examples and their explanations so it works without the poster or a digital link.

A further contrast addresses evidence: “The building used this verified amount during this period” versus “This does not establish how much this action would save.” Use an actual aggregate figure only when its scope and units can be explained clearly. Do not invent an action-level estimate for the sake of the example. If an estimate is supported, explain what assumptions would have to hold and why the actual result may differ.

Invite readers to identify the situation closest to their visit, while acknowledging that none may apply. Use ordinary, neutral language; avoid depicting people who make mistakes as careless or wasteful.

Implementation requires selecting genuinely contrasting policy cases, checking their accuracy and designing a readable pair of printed pieces. It assumes the policies contain meaningful boundaries that short examples can illustrate. Its strength is helping readers transfer a rule to a concrete situation. Its principal limitation is overgeneralization: readers may copy the visible action while overlooking the condition that permits it. Too many cases would also crowd the poster.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare the worked examples with a plain role-separated action list using the same policy facts and uncertainty statement. Give six to eight readers one familiar case and one new case governed by the same policy. Ask what they could do, why, and which part requires staff. Then ask for one feasible action during their own visit and what the energy figure establishes about savings. Reject or simplify the examples if readers succeed only on the copied case, miss authority boundaries, or treat measured consumption as a savings promise. Inspect whether the examples remain legible at the intended poster distance.

EXPAND.title: Explain how an action could affect energy use
EXPAND.proposal:
Build one printed poster and its take-home card around short causal explanations: permitted action → change in equipment operation → possible change in energy use. The mechanism is helping readers understand why an option might work and which conditions could prevent it from making a difference. This can support informed action without relying on a persuasive savings number.

Keep visibly separate “Visitors” and “Staff only” sections. Each contains one or two policy-supported actions, a plain explanation of the energy pathway and a relevant condition. For instance, switching off designated equipment could reduce its operating time, but the actual saving depends on its power demand, how long it would otherwise run and any automatic controls. Include that example only if the policies establish that visitors may control the equipment. Staff pathways must reflect actions within staff authority, without promising that every suggested adjustment is operationally appropriate.

The card repeats the complete explanations and role boundaries. Invite readers to choose an action whose conditions fit their situation, including the option that none applies. Do not use fear, moral judgments or unsupported rankings.

Verified aggregate figures may appear as clearly dated building context, but must not be presented as evidence that a particular pathway has delivered savings. State that a plausible mechanism does not establish its magnitude here. If no supported estimate exists, say the savings have not been quantified; if one exists, retain its assumptions and uncertainty.

Implementation needs policy verification, technically sound explanations and printing. General knowledge can explain the pathway, but cannot establish local equipment behavior. The approach assumes a few pathways can be described accurately without technical investigation. Its strength is giving readers a reason for acting; its limits are reading burden and the risk that an intuitive explanation sounds more certain than the local evidence warrants.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare the causal-explanation pair with a simple role-separated list containing the same actions and savings caveat. Ask six readers to identify one feasible action, explain how it could affect energy use and name a condition under which its benefit would be smaller or uncertain. Ask who controls each action and whether the aggregate figure verifies its savings. Revise or reject this mechanism if explanations increase unjustified confidence, cause readers to infer unsupported savings numbers, or obscure feasible actions. A successful check would support clearer understanding, not demonstrate actual energy reduction.

EXPAND.title: A private recall-and-correct prompt
EXPAND.proposal:
Use one printed poster and a folded take-home card to turn passive reading into a brief, private rehearsal. The mechanism is retrieval with immediate correction: readers try to name an authorized action and explain what the evidence means, then check their answers. This could expose misunderstandings that fluent reading leaves unnoticed.

The poster presents a short, policy-verified action list in clearly separate “Visitors” and “Staff only” sections. Below it, invite readers to look away and answer: “What is one action you could take here, and when is it allowed?” Accept “None fits this visit” as a legitimate answer. A second prompt asks: “Can the building’s recorded energy use tell us how much that action saves?” The printed explanation states that aggregate consumption alone cannot establish action-level savings.

The card places the same prompts outside and the complete action list, role boundaries and evidence explanation inside. Readers can attempt an answer before opening it; participation is optional, answers are not collected, and the language avoids scores or judgments. If a supported savings estimate is included, its assumptions and uncertainty appear beside it on both pieces. Otherwise explicitly state that savings have not been quantified.

Implementation requires policy screening, plain-language editing, a foldable card layout and printing. It assumes readers will spend a little time attempting recall and that the selected actions have conditions short enough to check accurately. Its advantage is making readers actively reconstruct both feasibility and uncertainty. Its limits are participation burden, possible discomfort with a quiz-like format, and the possibility of remembering an incorrect answer without checking. Successful recall would show comprehension, not actual energy savings.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare the prototype with a plain action-menu poster and card containing identical facts. Ask a small convenience sample of visitors and staff to inspect one version, then close it. Ask each person to name one action feasible within their role and explain its permission boundary, or correctly explain why none applies. Ask what the stated building figure or savings estimate establishes and what remains uncertain. Record explanations without personal usage data. The mechanism is challenged if recall-and-correct produces no clearer answers than the menu, increases skipped reading, or leaves readers confidently repeating errors. Treat this as an initial usability check, not proof of effectiveness.
